accuracy.reason: All nine objectives are taught accurately: key-value identity is independent of cache role/durability; operation results are distinguished from failures; namespacing is not authorization; query access paths, atomic conflicts, uncertain retries, lifetime, distribution and workload fit retain their implementation-specific limits. Every distinct source was read with primary followups where the slide URL covered only part of its claims.

evidence.quote: The key-value label says nothing by itself about whether acknowledged writes survive a crash. Check the store's persistence settings and failure guarantees before using it as the only copy.
Concerns whether acknowledged data survives specified failures. A durable write can still be absent from a lagging read. Conversely, seeing a new value does not prove that it will survive a crash.

mechanisms.reason: Names caller, key, value and store, traces replacement/deletion and lost updates, then shows why an indivisible version check rejects the stale writer. Retry identity and atomic effect coordination explain duplicate prevention; expiry and lagging reads have explicit causes. Both diagrams correctly depict namespace identity versus permission and a rejected stale version followed by reread/recompute.

evidence.quote: Tests a condition and changes the value as one indivisible operation. With version checking, a caller supplies the version it read; the store writes only if that version still matches, and advances it on success.

To prevent duplicate increments, the system must recognize the same logical operation and prevent a second effect. Keep the same ID and intent on retries. A request ID alone is insufficient: recording it and changing the data must be coordinated atomically, with duplicate records retained for the retry window. Verify the product's actual support and scope.

coherence.reason: Model and operation semantics precede identity/query design, then concurrency precedes retries, followed by lifetime and distributed guarantees before selection. All nine card objectives and every card criterion have local explanations; no recurring narrative is needed. The distinctions remain consistent in both diagrams and actual learner transfer.

evidence.quote: A key selects data; it does not grant permission. Verify the caller's access to the organization and record before reading or changing it. A guessed key must not bypass that check.

Before selecting it, verify authorization, value size and traffic distribution, concurrent-update and retry behavior, required read freshness, durability and retention. Explain which requirements matter for this workload and what happens when the store is unavailable.

decisions.reason: Teaches when independent known-key records fit and why changing filters/joins impose scan, index or coordination costs. It supplies concrete choices for value boundaries, authorization, conflict retries, uncertain effects, authoritative retention and read/durability requirements. The learner selects and justifies authorization and concurrency checks without claiming the model guarantees performance.

evidence.quote: An index takes storage and update work. When a record moves cities or is deleted, the index must change too. Check who maintains it and when its results reflect writes; an application-maintained index adds coordination work.

Joins combine related records. Frequent joins or new filters over value fields need more than basic key lookup. Scans read extra data; indexes and duplicated records add update work; application-side joins add requests and coordination.

clarity.reason: Introduces key, value, namespace, scan, index, atomic conditional write, idempotent effect, TTL, eviction, partition, hot key, consistency and durability at use. Small replacement and counter examples expose the relevant differences; all actual learner evidence strings match and entail their associated claims. Detail remains within the stated API/database prerequisites.

evidence.quote: A get timeout means no result arrived. It does not tell you whether the key exists. Keep operational failures separate from confirmed absence; turning an outage into 'not found' can create incorrect replacement data.

Expiration is also not a scheduler promising that business work runs at the exact deadline. Enforce an access deadline when authorizing use, and use a suitable work-execution mechanism for timed actions.

outcomes.reason: Actual learner meets all five criteria: known-key lookup with consistently escaped tenant/device/kind identity and complete settings value; authoritative versus disposable-cache role with verified persistence; replacement removes color and deletion observed by the read yields absence; timeout remains unknown; authorization remains separate. Slides1-3 explicitly teach each step and the namespace diagram preserves the permission boundary.

Learner explains why region is not the equipment ID, why scanning work follows inspected entries rather than matches, and how a region-to-IDs index locates candidates. It covers storage/update work, changes and deletions, maintenance ownership, visibility and implementation-specific availability. All four criteria and the more detailed card criteria are supported by slide4 evidence.

Learner traces 20/version7 to competing blind21 writes and lost intended22, then one conditional success with advanced version and one rejection. Reread, recomputation to22 and a fresh conditional attempt preserve the rejected intent if contention permits. It explains the separate-check race and bounds retries; all four criteria follow slide5 and its correct 10/version4 diagram. No universal multi-key protection is inferred.

Learner identifies uncertain execution, same-value replacement under the no-intervening-write assumption and duplicate atomic increments. It requires verified stable-operation duplicate protection with atomic effect/receipt and retry-window retention, otherwise avoids a blind retry. It separately explains expiry, possible earlier capacity eviction, no retention/refresh/exact-time-work guarantee and product-specific visibility/configuration. All six criteria are supported; no concrete recovery implementation is required by this objective.

Learner locally defines partitions, explains many-key load spreading versus concentrated hot-key capacity, and distinguishes lagging-read visibility from survival after failures. It requires checking implementation, persistence/replication and selected operation modes before either promise. All five criteria are supported without importing a consensus or routing mechanism the lesson does not teach.

Learner selects known-key independent preferences as the direct fit and explains extra scan reads, index maintenance and application-join coordination for changing filters/joins. Its two explicit checks are authorization against guessed-key exposure and atomic concurrent-update protection against lost changes. It rejects speed/safety conclusions from labels and asks for representative measurement. All four criteria are supported by slides3,5,9.

sourceChecks.claim: AWS core components establishes unique primary-key item identity and structured attributes. Supplemental Redis persistence https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/persistence/ explicitly permits disabled persistence for caching and documents snapshot/AOF loss tradeoffs; this supports distinguishing access model, authoritative/cache role and verified durability.

GetItem distinguishes returned item from a successful response without an Item and documents read modes. Supplemental https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/APIReference/API_PutItem.html verifies full replacement and permitted empty non-key values; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/APIReference/API_DeleteItem.html verifies removal. AWS error documentation distinguishes operational failure from results. The lesson correctly qualifies reads that observe deletion.

The linked IAM conditions page verifies that item/attribute permission requires an identity-bound policy, not knowledge of a primary key. Core components and the NoSQL design page support unique identities and access-pattern-oriented records. Tenant/kind separation and consistent escaping are direct identity-collision reasoning; value transfer/replacement costs follow actual bytes and documented item-size-sensitive capacity. The diagram shows two distinct identities and explicitly retains permission checks.

The index page verifies alternate keys, projected primary keys, maintained updates, read-consistency differences and write-capacity costs. Supplemental https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Scan.html explicitly says filtering follows reads and does not reduce consumed capacity. Basic lookup alone does not create these optional access paths; the conceptual candidate-ID index is not falsely presented as every vendor API.

ConditionExpressions verifies conditional put acceptance/rejection. Supplemental https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/DynamoDBMapper.OptimisticLocking.html establishes version matching, advancement and reread after conflict; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/WorkingWithItems.html confirms atomic operations and current-state conditional writes. The lost-update example and diagram correctly preserve one atomic boundary and do not extend it to external effects.

AWS errors explicitly says a failed write response can conceal success and recommends checking state/conditions or documented idempotency; it separates retryable failures and backoff. WorkingWithItems explicitly distinguishes non-idempotent atomic counters. AWS Builders Library https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/ was actually checked earlier in this reviewer session for the same stable identity/intent, atomic recording-plus-effect and retention-window claims. The lesson conditions product support and offers avoiding blind retries.

DynamoDB TTL explicitly documents delayed background deletion and still-accessible expired items; it is not an exact-deadline execution service. Supplemental https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/eviction/ documents memory-triggered, configured eviction, including keys with remaining TTL and noeviction mode. Thus lifetime does not promise retention or refresh, and authorization deadlines require independent enforcement.

The partition-key design source documents per-partition limits, item-size effects and uniform activity rather than key counts. Supplemental https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/HowItWorks.Partitions.html defines distributed storage partitions; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/HowItWorks.ReadConsistency.html distinguishes durable successful writes from eventually consistent reads missing recent changes. Redis persistence independently demonstrates that observed writes can be lost under some configurations. No universal hot-key or survival guarantee is made.

NoSQL design explicitly requires knowing access patterns and notes expensive queries outside supported paths. Combined checked scan/index/operation documentation substantiates extra reads, maintenance and coordination. The lesson appropriately treats richer-query products as a possible fit and requires correctness and representative workload checks instead of claiming universal speed or safety.
